newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Merger fresh twist in English Channel drama.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Merger fresh twist in English Channel drama.

text.p: Days after a controversial deal to rescue Eurotunnel from the brink of bankruptcy, two of its fiercest rivals, ferry lines P&O and Stena, raised the stakes on the busy English Channel crossing with a plan to merge.

Industry players said Thursday's merger plan emphasised the three companies' interdependence and noted that the ferries' long-term commercial success could still hinge on Anglo-French Eurotunnel helping to end a current price war.

Analysts said that sustained, strong growth in the market for transport across the narrow gap between England and northern France and Belgium was the only reason all three had made it this far, after a bloodbath year for the ferries especially.

Even if the P&O-Stena Line joint venture proceeds as planned and the two combine sailings and marketing for their ships joining Dover, Newhaven, Calais, Dieppe and Zeebrugge, they saw the situation remaining tense until Eurotunnel stabilises.

"I think that post the refinancing of Eurotunnel it's highly unlikely that (transport) rates stay down in the bargain basement where they have been this year," said Selwyn Jones, transport analyst at Credit Lyonnais Lang in London.
"It's been no good for Eurotunnel and no good for P&O and Stena," he added, noting that the Swedish company has lost money on the key Dover/Calais run and P&O "is barely profitable".

But Jones said it was hard to tell when Eurotunnel would change, and thus to predict the level of any rate increase next year, especially in the vital summer season between May and September when passenger volumes are highest.

The true financial picture for Eurotunnel is still unknown as it moves towards a deal that is expected to swap about half of its 9.0 billion pounds ($14 billion) outstanding debt for new equity and bonds. Details are due to be revealed next Monday.
Debt analysts have said that even when the path forwards is clear a final deal may not be agreed and implemented until next spring, meaning months of uncertainty.
Nevertheless, channel watchers told Reuters they felt Eurotunnel will have to drag itself back into the real world and start to rebuild pricing, helping rebuild the ferries' health.
"Over a period it will be in everybody's interests just to recover some of the monies that have been given away at the margin," said NatWest Markets analyst Mark McVicar.
"That will get everyone back on their feet," he added, but like the others would not be drawn on how soon it may happen.

In the short term, however, analysts agreed the proposed P&O Stena Line joint venture would bring some gains for the partners, anyway, as it would present the two parent firms with a sustainable cost base and attractive economies of scale.
The pair have already predicted they could slash 75 million pounds off a combined fixed cost base of 280 million just for starters, and they foresee strong cash generation.
At present, P&O and Stena say their joint share of the one of the world's biggest short-haul surface transport markets is very close to Eurotunnel's 45 percent, based on August figures.

Eurotunnel intends to add freight car capacity and build up its efficiency, with some market analysts predicting it will push its share on towards 60 percent, so threatening to outgrow even the strongest ferry line.

However, organic volume growth in the whole market is still running at the annual rate of 15 to 20 percent seen in recent years, and analysts say this will remain the ferries' lifeline. ($1=.6388 Pound)
